Stroke Syndromes

Localization, recognition, and acute management — master the vascular territories, recognize the patterns, localize the lesion.
Alexandra Filippakis, D.O.  ·  Greenleaf Neurology, PLLC  ·  Notes built from slides + live lecture transcript
01

Stroke Fundamentals & Classification

Stroke questions on boards are localization questions. Master the vascular territories, recognize the patterns, and the diagnosis falls out on its own.

Two Types of Stroke

Ischemic (~87%)

A clot blocks arterial flow → downstream infarction.

Hemorrhagic (~13%)

Vessel rupture → intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Board Pearl
Clinical symptoms alone CANNOT distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke — brain imaging is required, every time, before you can tell them apart.

TOAST Classification of Ischemic Stroke

TOAST = Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment. This is how stroke neurologists actually talk to each other — "stroke" alone means nothing; the mechanism is the whole conversation.

SubtypeKey FeaturesSecondary Prevention
Large artery atherosclerosis≥50% stenosis; large cortical/subcortical infarctCEA/stenting; antiplatelets; statins
CardioembolismAFib, valvular disease; wedge-shaped, may be bilateralAnticoagulation (DOACs)
Small vessel (lacunar)Subcortical <1.5 cm; classic lacunar syndromeAntiplatelets; BP control
Other determinedDissection, vasculitis, hypercoagulableTreat underlying cause
CryptogenicNo cause found despite full workupAntiplatelets; consider PFO closure (age 18–60)

Board Pearl: Cardioembolism Clues

Suspect cardioembolism when you see:

  • Infarcts in BOTH hemispheres
  • Infarcts in BOTH anterior AND posterior circulations
  • Wedge-shaped, cortical infarcts
  • Known AFib, mechanical valve, recent MI, endocarditis
"Think about it mechanically — if you have a stenotic left M1 segment, you get one left MCA syndrome. The only way you get strokes on the left AND right, anterior AND posterior, simultaneously, is if the clot is coming from a proximal source — the heart or the aortic arch — throwing off a shower of emboli."

Risk Factors

Modifiable

  • Hypertension — #1, most important for BOTH ischemic and hemorrhagic
  • Diabetes, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation
  • Smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle

Non-Modifiable

  • Age
  • Sex
  • Race/ethnicity
  • Family history
Case Warm-Up

A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden-onset right hemiparesis and aphasia. CT head shows no hemorrhage.

1. What type of stroke?   2. What TOAST subtype?   3. What secondary prevention?

Work through the three questions above, then check your reasoning.
Ischemic stroke (no blood on CT) → Cardioembolism (known AFib is the giveaway) → Anticoagulation (DOAC preferred over warfarin).
02

Cerebrovascular Anatomy

If you know this anatomy well and can draw it from memory, localizing stroke syndromes becomes fairly easy.

Anterior Circulation (Internal Carotid)

  • ACA → medial cortex
  • MCA → lateral cortex

Posterior Circulation (Vertebrobasilar)

  • PCA → occipital, inferior temporal, thalamus
  • PICA, AICA, SCA → cerebellum, brainstem
Cerebrovascular Anatomy Internal carotid → ACA (medial cortex) + MCA (lateral cortex). Vertebrobasilar system → PCA (occipital, inferior temporal, thalamus) + PICA/AICA/SCA (cerebellum, brainstem). Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis
Vascular Territories ACA (blue) = medial surface → LEG. MCA (red) = lateral surface → FACE & ARM. PCA (green) = posterior/inferior → VISION & THALAMUS. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis
Board Pearl
The MCA territory = ~54% of supratentorial volume → the most commonly affected vessel in stroke.

The Homunculus & Vascular Supply

Homunculus & Vascular Supply ACA supplies the medial cortex → LEG area of the homunculus. MCA supplies the lateral cortex → FACE and ARM area. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis
Board Pearl
"Leg > arm" = ACA  |  "Face/arm > leg" = MCA

Circle of Willis: Aneurysm Sites

Common Aneurysm Sites 1. Anterior communicating artery (AComm) — #1 most common. 2. Posterior communicating artery (PComm) — #2. 3. MCA bifurcation — #3. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis
03

MCA & ACA Syndromes

MCA Stroke: Overview

Most common stroke territory. Complete MCA syndrome:

  • Contralateral hemiparesis (face & arm >> leg)
  • Contralateral hemisensory loss (face & arm >> leg)
  • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia
  • Eyes deviate TOWARD the lesion
  • Plus cortical signs (aphasia / neglect / hemianopia)

MCA Stroke: Dominant vs. Non-Dominant

Dominant (usually LEFT)

  • Broca's aphasia (frontal — nonfluent)
  • Wernicke's aphasia (temporal — fluent)
  • Global aphasia (large territory)
  • Gerstmann syndrome (angular gyrus)

Non-Dominant (usually RIGHT)

  • Hemispatial neglect (parietal)
  • Anosognosia (unaware of deficit)
  • Constructional apraxia
Board Pearl
Aphasia = dominant hemisphere.  |  Neglect = non-dominant hemisphere.

Gerstmann Syndrome

Lesion: dominant (left) angular gyrus, MCA territory. The four components:

  1. Agraphia (cannot write)
  2. Acalculia (cannot calculate)
  3. Finger agnosia (cannot identify fingers)
  4. Left-right confusion

Broca vs. Wernicke Aphasia

FeatureBroca'sWernicke's
LocationInferior frontal gyrusSuperior temporal gyrus
FluencyNon-fluent (broken, effortful)Fluent (word salad, neologisms)
ComprehensionIntactImpaired
RepetitionImpairedImpaired
AwarenessAware (frustrated)Unaware
MCA divisionSuperiorInferior
"Broca's area sits right next to primary motor cortex — hit that area, you hit motor fibers too. Wernicke's is further back, so no motor fibers involved. That's the anatomy question hiding behind 'why does Wernicke's aphasia have no weakness?'"

Deep MCA Infarct

Lenticulostriate arteries → basal ganglia, internal capsule.

  • Pure motor hemiparesis (face = arm = leg)
  • NO cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect, no hemianopia)
  • Overlaps with lacunar syndromes
Case: MCA Stroke

A 72-year-old right-handed woman presents with right face/arm weakness, right homonymous hemianopia, and speaks fluently but makes no sense.

1. Where is the lesion?   2. What artery?   3. What type of aphasia?

Work it through, then check.
Left MCA, inferior division → Wernicke's aphasia. (Right-handed = left dominant; fluent-but-nonsensical speech = Wernicke's, which localizes to the inferior MCA division.)

ACA Stroke: Overview

ACA supplies medial frontal and parietal cortex.

  • Contralateral LEG weakness and sensory loss >> arm
  • Urinary incontinence (loss of frontal inhibition)
  • Behavioral changes: abulia, apathy, akinetic mutism
  • Transcortical motor aphasia (dominant hemisphere) — repetition is intact, unlike Broca's/Wernicke's
  • Alien hand syndrome (corpus callosum)
  • Grasp reflex
Board Pearl
ACA infarcts = only ~3% of ischemic strokes, despite being high-yield on exams.

ACA vs. MCA — Side by Side

FeatureACAMCA
Weakness patternLeg >> arm/faceFace/arm >> leg
Sensory loss patternLeg >> arm/faceFace/arm >> leg
LanguageTranscortical motor aphasiaBroca's, Wernicke's, or global
BehavioralAbulia, alien handNeglect (non-dominant)
IncontinenceYesNo
Frequency~3%Most common
Case: ACA Stroke

A 72-year-old woman presents with left leg weakness, urinary incontinence, and flat affect. Arm strength is 5/5. Face is symmetric.

Where is the lesion?

Localize it.
Right ACA territory — isolated leg weakness with incontinence and behavioral flattening, full arm strength, symmetric face.
04

Lacunar Syndromes

Small (<1.5 cm) subcortical infarcts from a single penetrating artery occlusion — lipohyalinosis from chronic hypertension, or microatheroma. About 25% of all ischemic strokes.

Cardinal Rule
Lacunar strokes have NO cortical signs — no aphasia, no neglect, no hemianopia. They're deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons), not cortical.
"C. Miller Fisher — a legendary neurologist at Mass General, sort of the father of stroke — described these five patterns decades ago from watching exactly where small-vessel strokes landed. It's worth learning them as a set."

The 5 Classic Lacunar Syndromes

SyndromeClinical FeaturesLocation
Pure motor hemiparesis ★Face/arm/leg weakness; no sensory lossPosterior limb internal capsule, pons
Pure sensory strokeFace/arm/leg numbness; no weaknessVPL nucleus of thalamus
Sensorimotor strokeHemiparesis + hemisensory lossThalamocapsular junction
Ataxic hemiparesisWeakness + ipsilateral limb ataxia (same side)Pons, internal capsule
Dysarthria-clumsy handDysarthria + hand clumsinessGenu of internal capsule, pons

★ = Most common lacunar syndrome

Case: Lacunar Stroke

A 65-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with equal weakness of the right face, arm, and leg. No aphasia, no neglect, no visual field cut. Sensation is intact.

1. What type of stroke?   2. Where is the lesion?

Localize it.
Pure motor hemiparesis (lacunar stroke) → left posterior limb of the internal capsule. Equal face/arm/leg weakness with zero cortical signs is the giveaway.
Hour 1 Summary — Localization Rules
  • Face/arm > leg weakness + aphasia → Left MCA
  • Face/arm > leg weakness + neglect → Right MCA
  • Leg > arm weakness + abulia/incontinence → ACA
  • Equal face/arm/leg, NO cortical signs → Lacunar
05

Posterior Circulation & Thalamic Syndromes

PCA Stroke: Overview

PCA supplies: occipital lobe, inferior temporal lobe, thalamus, midbrain. Cortical PCA stroke:

  • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (most common finding)
  • Macular sparing (dual blood supply — MCA also feeds the macula)
  • Visual agnosia, prosopagnosia
  • Alexia without agraphia (left PCA)
  • Memory impairment

Alexia Without Agraphia — "Can Write but Cannot Read"

Mechanism: a left PCA stroke destroys (1) the left visual cortex → right homonymous hemianopia, and (2) the splenium of the corpus callosum → visual info from the intact right occipital cortex can't reach the left angular gyrus (the reading center).

Result: writing is preserved (motor pathways intact), but reading is impossible — the patient writes a perfect sentence, then cannot read back what they just wrote.

Thalamic Stroke Syndromes

Dejerine-Roussy Syndrome (Thalamic Pain Syndrome)

  • Initial: contralateral sensory loss — patients often describe it as "being cut in half"
  • Weeks later: severe burning contralateral pain (neuropathic — treat with gabapentin, etc.)
  • Thalamic aphasia (dominant side)
  • Paramedian thalamic infarct → somnolence, behavioral changes ("top of the basilar") — high mortality, rapid loss of consciousness

Visual Field Deficits by Location

LesionVisual Field Deficit
Optic nerveMonocular vision loss (ipsilateral)
Optic chiasmBitemporal hemianopia
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop)Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
Parietal lobeContralateral inferior quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor")
Occipital lobe (PCA)Contralateral homonymous hemianopia +/- macular sparing
Visual Pathway & Field Defects Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations → occipital cortex. Where the pathway is disrupted determines the exact field-cut pattern. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis
06

Brainstem Syndromes

Big Principle
CROSSED FINDINGS = BRAINSTEM. Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit + contralateral motor/sensory deficit. Why? Cranial nerve nuclei sit in the brainstem, but the long tracts (corticospinal, spinothalamic) cross.

Cranial Nerve Levels

LevelCranial Nerves
MidbrainCN III, IV
PonsCN V, VI, VII, VIII
MedullaCN IX, X, XI, XII

"3, 4 — midbrain floor"   "5, 6, 7, 8 — pons is great"   "9, 10, 11, 12 — medulla helps you swallow and shelve"

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenberg) ★

THE highest-yield brainstem syndrome for boards — and genuinely common on the wards. Artery: PICA or vertebral artery.

Lateral Medullary Syndrome Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII), nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X), spinal trigeminal nucleus (CN V), spinothalamic tract, and descending sympathetics all sit in the lateral medulla — everything a PICA/vertebral occlusion can hit. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis

Wallenberg: Structure → Symptom

StructureFinding
Vestibular nucleiVertigo, nausea, nystagmus
Inferior cerebellar peduncleIpsilateral ataxia
Spinal trigeminal nucleus (CN V)Ipsilateral face pain/temp loss
Spinothalamic tractContralateral body pain/temp loss
Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X)Dysphagia, hoarseness
Descending sympatheticsIpsilateral Horner syndrome
Board Pearl
NO motor weakness — the corticospinal tract is medial and spared. Crossed sensory loss: ipsilateral face + contralateral body.
"PICA Don't LIE" Lateral medullary syndrome; Ipsilateral face + contralateral body (pain/temp); Everything EXCEPT motor. (Dr. Filippakis's own 4th-year-med-school Facebook profile picture — the "armchair intellectual" neurology cartoon.) Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis

Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine)

Artery: anterior spinal artery or vertebral branches. Much less common than Wallenberg, but still testable.

Medial Medullary Syndrome Pyramidal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII) sit medially — the classic triad of an ASA/vertebral branch occlusion. Stroke Syndromes, Filippakis

Classic Triad

  1. Contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid/corticospinal tract)
  2. Contralateral proprioception/vibration loss (medial lemniscus)
  3. Ipsilateral tongue deviation (CN XII) — a lower motor neuron CN XII palsy; tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion

Lateral vs. Medial Medullary Syndrome

FeatureLateral (Wallenberg)Medial (Dejerine)
ArteryPICA / vertebralASA / vertebral branches
Motor weaknessNOYES (contralateral)
Sensory modalityPain/temperatureProprioception/vibration
Cranial nerveIX, X (dysphagia)XII (tongue deviation)
Horner syndromeYesNo
VertigoYesNo
FrequencyCommonRare
Case: Wallenberg

A 55-year-old man presents with vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, left Horner syndrome, left facial numbness to pinprick, and right body numbness to pinprick. No weakness.

1. What syndrome?   2. What artery?   3. Why no weakness?

Work it through.
Left Wallenberg syndrome → left PICA/vertebral artery. No weakness because the corticospinal tract is medial and spared.

Locked-In Syndrome — Key Distinction

Board Pearl
Locked-in ≠ coma. Artery: basilar artery occlusion → bilateral ventral pons. Complete quadriplegia + anarthria, but consciousness is PRESERVED (the reticular activating system in the tegmentum is spared). Only voluntary movement: vertical eye movements + blinking (CN III sits in the midbrain, above the lesion).
"Locked-in is not a coma — a coma would honestly be better. The patient is fully aware, they can hear everything, they just can't move or speak except for their eyes. It's one of the most devastating things to witness in neurology."

AICA Syndrome (Lateral Pontine)

Artery: anterior inferior cerebellar artery. Similar to Wallenberg but at the pontine level:

  • Ipsilateral facial paralysis (CN VII)
  • Ipsilateral hearing loss (CN VIII) — the distinguishing feature
  • Ipsilateral facial sensory loss (CN V)
  • Contralateral body pain/temp loss
  • Ipsilateral Horner, ataxia
Board Pearl
Hearing loss = AICA (not PICA).

Midbrain Syndromes

SyndromeStructuresFindings
WeberCN III + cerebral peduncleIpsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
BenediktCN III + red nucleusIpsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral tremor
ClaudeCN III + SCP + red nucleusIpsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia + tremor
ParinaudPretectum / superior colliculusParalysis of upward gaze, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus
Board Pearl
Weber = "motor" (peduncle)  |  Benedikt = "movement" (red nucleus)
Case: Midbrain Stroke

A patient has left ptosis, left eye "down and out," left dilated pupil, and right-sided weakness of face, arm, and leg.

1. What syndrome?   2. What level?

Localize it.
Weber syndrome → left midbrain (CN III + cerebral peduncle).

Eye Deviation in Stroke

Lesion LocationEyes Deviate...Explanation
Cortical (e.g. MCA)TOWARD the lesionFrontal eye field destroyed → unopposed contralateral FEF pushes eyes toward lesion
PontineAWAY from the lesion (toward weakness)PPRF destroyed → eyes pushed away
ThalamicDOWNWARD ("peering at the nose")Pressure on midbrain tectum
Board Pearl
"Cortex looks at the lesion; pons looks at the weakness."
07

Watershed Infarcts & Hemorrhagic Stroke

Watershed (Border Zone) Infarcts

Occur at junctions between arterial territories — the lowest perfusion pressure zones. Causes: severe hypotension, cardiac arrest, severe carotid stenosis.

TypeLocationPresentation
External (cortical)ACA/MCA or MCA/PCA border"Man in a barrel" — bilateral proximal arm weakness
Internal (subcortical)Deep perforators vs. cortical branches"String of pearls" on imaging
Case: Watershed Infarct

A patient undergoes cardiac surgery and wakes up unable to lift either arm at the shoulder, but can wiggle fingers and move both legs.

What happened?

Think it through.
Bilateral ACA-MCA watershed infarcts — "man in a barrel" syndrome, from perioperative hypoperfusion during/around cardiac surgery.

Hemorrhagic Stroke: ICH Locations

Most common cause: hypertension. In descending frequency:

  1. Putamen / basal ganglia (most common) — lenticulostriate arteries
  2. Thalamus
  3. Pons
  4. Cerebellum
  5. Lobar (less commonly hypertensive)
Board Pearl
A lobar hemorrhage in an elderly patient → think cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Recurrent lobar hemorrhages; associated with Alzheimer disease; Congo red stain → apple-green birefringence.

Cerebellar Hemorrhage — Emergency

Clinical: sudden headache, vomiting, severe ataxia, inability to walk. Danger: compresses the 4th ventricle → obstructive hydrocephalus → herniation → death.

Board Pearl
Cerebellar hemorrhage >3 cm or with hydrocephalus → EMERGENT SURGICAL EVACUATION. This is a "call neurosurgery immediately" moment.
08

Acute Stroke Management

Initial Assessment

  1. ABCs
  2. Check glucose (hypoglycemia is a stroke mimic!)
  3. Non-contrast CT head — FIRST imaging study
  4. NIHSS assessment (0–42 scale)
  5. Determine time of onset / last known well
Board Pearl
CT is done to EXCLUDE hemorrhage, not to confirm ischemia — ischemic stroke may not be visible on CT for 6–12 hours.
"'Last known well' matters enormously because so many strokes are wake-up strokes — someone went to bed fine and woke up not fine. We used to write these patients off as outside the treatment window. Now we know most wake-up strokes actually happen shortly before waking, around 4 a.m., so with the right imaging many of these patients are still treatable."

NIHSS: Key Points

  • National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale — 11 domains, score 0–42
  • 0 = no symptoms  |  1–4 = minor stroke  |  5–15 = moderate
  • 16–20 = moderate-severe  |  21–42 = severe stroke
Board Pearl
NIHSS is weighted toward anterior circulation / left hemisphere — posterior circulation strokes (e.g. basilar occlusion) may score deceptively LOW despite severe deficits.

IV Thrombolysis (tPA / Tenecteplase)

Window & Drug

  • Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (or last known well)
  • Tenecteplase (TNK): single IV bolus, increasingly preferred over alteplase infusion

Key Contraindications

  • Active internal bleeding
  • Recent intracranial surgery/trauma (within 3 months)
  • History of ICH
  • Platelets <100,000
  • INR >1.7 or PT >15 seconds
  • BP >185/110 (must lower first)
  • Glucose <50 mg/dL
Board Pearl
"Time is brain" — ~1.9 million neurons die per minute in an untreated large-vessel occlusion.

Mechanical Thrombectomy

Standard Window (≤6 hrs)

  • Large vessel occlusion (ICA or proximal MCA/M1)
  • NIHSS ≥6
  • ASPECTS ≥6 — Class I evidence

Extended Window (6–24 hrs)

  • Select patients with perfusion imaging (DAWN, DEFUSE 3 trials)
  • Must show a salvageable penumbra — mismatch between core infarct and at-risk tissue
Board Pearl
NNT = 2.6 to reduce disability by ≥1 level on the modified Rankin Scale — one of the most effective treatments in all of medicine.
"I watched an administrator collapse with a severe left MCA stroke right in front of eight neurologists at a staff meeting about a mile from our hospital. Door-to-needle time was something like 12 minutes. NIH stroke scale in the 20s. Five days later she walked out of the hospital and went back to work. That's what timely intervention actually looks like — we're not just armchair intellectuals localizing lesions for fun."

Secondary Prevention

Stroke SubtypePrevention Strategy
Cardioembolic (AFib)Anticoagulation (DOACs preferred)
Large artery atherosclerosisCEA/stenting if ≥50% symptomatic; antiplatelets; high-intensity statin
Lacunar / small vesselAntiplatelets; BP control (<130/80)
Minor stroke / high-risk TIADAPT (ASA + clopidogrel) × 21 days → single antiplatelet
Cryptogenic (age 18–60 with PFO)Consider PFO closure
All Patients
High-intensity statin, LDL goal <70 mg/dL. "PCPs, don't give me simvastatin 20 mg — we need Lipitor 80 or Crestor 40, high-intensity, full stop."
09

Localization Tables & Top 10 Board Pearls

Localization Table (1 of 2)

FindingLocalization
Face/arm weakness > leg + aphasiaLeft MCA
Face/arm weakness > leg + neglectRight MCA
Leg weakness > arm + abuliaACA
Homonymous hemianopia +/- macular sparingPCA
Pure motor hemiparesis, no cortical signsLacunar (internal capsule / pons)

Localization Table (2 of 2)

FindingLocalization
Crossed findings (ipsilateral CN + contralateral body)Brainstem
Vertigo + dysphagia + Horner + crossed sensory, NO weaknessWallenberg (PICA / lateral medulla)
Ipsilateral CN III + contralateral hemiparesisWeber (midbrain)
Quadriplegia + anarthria + preserved consciousnessLocked-in (basilar / bilateral ventral pons)
Bilateral proximal arm weakness after hypotensionWatershed (ACA-MCA border zone)
Alexia without agraphiaLeft PCA
Top 10 Board Pearls
  1. Clinical symptoms CANNOT distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic → need imaging
  2. MCA = face/arm > leg  |  ACA = leg > arm
  3. Aphasia = dominant hemisphere  |  Neglect = non-dominant
  4. Lacunar = NO cortical signs
  5. Crossed findings = brainstem
  6. Wallenberg = PICA, lateral medulla, NO motor weakness
  7. Locked-in ≠ coma (consciousness preserved)
  8. Eyes look at the lesion (cortex) vs. away from the lesion (pons)
  9. CT is to EXCLUDE hemorrhage, not confirm ischemia
  10. Thrombectomy NNT = 2.6 — one of the best treatments in medicine

Key Mnemonics Summary

  • "Face/Arm = MCA; Leg = ACA" (homunculus)
  • "Lacunar = No cortical signs"
  • "Crossed = Brainstem"
  • "PICA don't LIE" (Lateral, Ipsilateral face/contralateral body, Everything except motor)
  • "Locked-in ≠ Coma"
  • "Eyes look at the lesion" (cortex) vs. "Eyes look at the weakness" (pons)
  • "Pie in the sky" (temporal/Meyer's loop) vs. "Pie on the floor" (parietal)
Quiz

Quiz Yourself — Rapid-Fire Board Questions

Every rapid-fire question from the lecture, gathered in one place. Work each one out before revealing.

1. Right face/arm weakness + fluent nonsensical speech + right hemianopia →?
Left MCA, inferior division → Wernicke's aphasia
2. Left leg weakness + left leg numbness + urinary incontinence →?
Right ACA territory
3. Right face/arm/leg weakness equally, no aphasia, no neglect →?
Left internal capsule → pure motor hemiparesis (lacunar)
4. Vertigo + left Horner + left face numb + right body numb + dysphagia, no weakness →?
Left Wallenberg syndrome → left PICA / vertebral artery
5. Quadriplegic, cannot speak, but awake and blinks on command →?
Locked-in syndrome → basilar artery occlusion
6. Left CN III palsy + right hemiparesis →?
Weber syndrome → left midbrain
7. Can write but cannot read + right hemianopia →?
Alexia without agraphia → left PCA territory

Case-Warm-Up & Full Case Recall

Case Warm-Up
68M with AFib, sudden-onset right hemiparesis + aphasia, CT shows no hemorrhage. What TOAST subtype?
Known AFib is the dead giveaway on boards → cardioembolic stroke → anticoagulation for secondary prevention.
MCA case: 72F right-handed, right face/arm weakness, right homonymous hemianopia, fluent-but-nonsensical speech. Lesion, artery, aphasia type?
Left MCA, inferior division → Wernicke's aphasia.
Lacunar case: 65M, poorly controlled HTN, equal right face/arm/leg weakness, no cortical signs, sensation intact. Stroke type and lesion?
Pure motor hemiparesis (lacunar) → left posterior limb of the internal capsule.
Wallenberg case: 55M, vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, left Horner, left facial numbness to pinprick, right body numbness to pinprick, no weakness. Syndrome, artery, and why no weakness?
Left Wallenberg syndrome → left PICA/vertebral artery. No weakness because the corticospinal tract runs medially and is spared in a lateral lesion.
Midbrain case: Left ptosis, left eye "down and out," left dilated pupil, right-sided face/arm/leg weakness. Syndrome and level?
Weber syndrome → left midbrain (CN III + cerebral peduncle).
Watershed case: Patient wakes from cardiac surgery unable to lift either arm at the shoulder but can wiggle fingers and move both legs. What happened?
Bilateral ACA-MCA watershed infarcts — "man in a barrel" syndrome, from perioperative hypoperfusion.
